content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
The paper applies ideas from message passing over a global graph between agents to perform multi-agent reinforcement learning. The algorithm SMAL is demonstrated on a suite of continuous control domains.

The paper is imprecise, unpolished and doesn't reflect the state-of-art fairly. It does not support as significant contribution. The current approach conditions the policy on the messages from other agents and therefore is a centralized controller. Experiments make comparison to methods that either support decentralized execution (MADDPG) or are single-agent RL techniques (TRPO) which is unfair. No comparison to other methods like [1,2] that learn to communicate between agents or even the introduced environments in those works. The claim that "messages and rewards are both necessary for collaboration" is unjustified from the experiments given the environment comes from [3] which did not allow any communication between agents and showed scaling to 10 agents compared to 4 agents in the current work.

[1]: https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.07736
[2]: https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09755
[3]: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-71682-4_5

display_title: We appreciate your review and thank you for pointing out our weaknesses in experiments.

content.title: We appreciate your review and thank you for pointing out our weaknesses in experiments.
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review.

We admit that the comparison is unfair because MADDPG supports decentralized execution while our method includes a centralized controller(Although every agent has its own policy network). We are adding two baselines in our experiment: Centralized MADDPG(centralized actor and critic) and IC3Net[1] and will update our paper after these experiments are finished. We miss the citations of the two papers when discussing communications in Multi-agent systems and will add them to Related works.

The ablation studies are shown in our paper(Table 1). The baselines are created by setting shared messages and rewards as zero. That demonstrates why shared messages and shared rewards are both essential for our method. The main contribution of our paper is introducing a graph that shares both messages and rewards between agents. 

Thank you for your suggestions on our experiment settings and we will update a revised version soon.

[1]: https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09755

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes a new way to perform multi-agent reinforcement learning via using a graph neural network like method to pass messages from agents. They show performance improvements over baseline techniques such as TRPO, DDPG, and also multi-agent algorithm MADDPG.

The problem is very interesting and I do like the experimental domains such as multi-walker. However, the experimental results lack comparison against a simple baseline and it is unclear how the proposed SMAL algorithm would perform against basic multi-agent RL techniques.

There are also various inaccurate or debatable claims in the paper.
In the first paragraph, the authors state that single-agent RL learns to fulfill goals without modeling the behaviors of others. This is clearly not the case as the most basic model-free approaches such as DQN agents may indeed learn to model other’s behaviors inside their policy networks.

A basic centralized multi-agent system would have action spaces N times A where A is the action space of a single agent. Learning would take observations from all agents and act jointly and in a coordinated manner (both centralized actor and centralized critic). This system however is not scalable to a large number of agents. However, it is still a good baseline to compare against. For example. How would a centralized multi-agent DDPG system work on multi-walker? e.g. with dimensions 4*24 ? I think it would be surprising if SMAL would be better than this baseline, what are authors thoughts/views on this?

First paragraph of page 2 suggest that SMAL is able to learn +ve and -ve weights to suggest whether an agents are collaborators or competitors. However, from sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, it appears that those bounds on v_ij are actually set by hand.

Positive/negatives weights on an edge is hardly a good indicator of collaboration/competition. I do not see a relationship between the two. Typically, collaboration or competition arise out of the reward function, e.g. whether it is a zero-sum game or a general-sum game.

In addition, the claim in 4.1.2 that it is ok to zero-out messages from ‘competitors’ are dubious. Why would it not be beneficial to infer additional information from messages of other adversarial agents?

display_title: Thank you for your constructive ideas, we will add two baselines to our comparison.

content.title: Thank you for your constructive ideas, we will add two baselines to our comparison.
content.comment:
We appreciate your careful review and constructive ideas.

(1)Debatable claims: the first paragraph mainly focuses on the discussion of single-agent RL, and our claim is indeed not accurate. Single-agent RL methods do model the environment as a whole, including the behaviors of others. We will double-check our paper to avoid inaccurate claims.

(2)We view the centralized MADDPG method(with centralized actor and centralized critic) as an important baseline under this setting. The graph in our method is a variant of a centralized executor. We are going on with the experiments of that baseline. Also, the baseline in [1] is to be compared. 

(3)We agree that collaboration or competition arises out of the reward function and indeed we set the bounds on v_ij in all three environments because they are general-sum games. What edges really infer are the extent to which agents should collaborate with each other(For example, 1 refers to deep cooperation and 0.1 refers to less cooperation). Also, when agents have no prior knowledge of the reward function, we are expecting them to figure out who are the competitors through edges. So, if we know that the environment is cooperative, we can bound v_ij to [0,1]. Meanwhile, if agents have collaborators and competitors at the same time, they need to infer who is their partner, so v_ij is bounded to [-1,1] under this circumstance.

(4)In 4.1.2 we claim that it is ok to zero-out messages from competitors. We also make a discussion in A.1. The reason is that in the competitive setting, agents may generate messages to cheat their competitors.  [1] also shows that agents learn to stop communication in competitive cases. We will add some discussion about that in our paper.

Thanks again for your review and advice for our paper.

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.09755

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
In this paper authors propose a framework for learning in multi-agent systems. Main contribution of the proposed framework is that it learns the communication structure between the agents, which improves the perfomance. In order to impose a structure authors use a graph neural network, which enables the agents to share information and rewards. They empirically show that their method is able to outperform Multi-agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG), Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) on Waterworld, Multi-Walker and Multi-Ant tasks.

I would recommend the paper to be accepted since the authors came up with an innovative solution to the difficult problem of how to coordinate in a multi-agent setting although they have a limited experimental setup. In order to improve the exposition I would recommend the authors provide more evidence along the lines of how the proposed method deals with indefinite number of agents problem. How does the performance change as more agents added to the task. They chose 4 in their experiments why that number was chosen? How does the gap between baseline methods vs. SMAL change as the number of agents increase?

content.title: Thank you for the review
content.comment:
Thank you for your careful review.  

As the agent numbers of our simulators can be changed, we chose 4 in our experiments because the average rewards for agents are relatively high, which indicated that cooperation between 4 agents was enough(Considering the computational cost). Dealing with an indefinite number of agents is the ultimate goal for our method, which requires a major revision to the code of the simulator. If time is allowed, we will implement that after finishing the comparison experiments mentioned by Reviewer 1 and 2.

content.title: Paper Revision
content.comment:
We appreciate all the reviewers for their helpful suggestions and careful review! We have finished several additional experiments. The main changes in the paper include:

(1) We added two baselines to the comparison section: Centralized MADDPG and IC3Net. Although Centralized MADDPG outperforms our method in all three domains, our method achieves a near-optimal result. Also, our method surpasses IC3Net because IC3Net mainly focuses on efficient communication and doesn't involve a reward sharing mechanism.
(2) We fixed several typos and imprecise claims in the paper and polished the figures.
(3) We added the missing citations pointed out by Reviewer 2 to Related works.
(4) We updated the Appendix for some further discussions about the competitive setting.

We think the most controversial part lies in the setting of the experiment and SMAL should be considered a method with a centralized executor. The policy of every agent is conditioned on messages from others.

MADDPG: centralized critics + decentralized executors
Centralized MADDPG: centralized critic + centralized executor
SMAL: centralized executor
